notes.meaning: Ephraim once held great honor and authority, and people trembled with respect whenever the tribe spoke. But when the nation turned to the worship of Baal, a false god, they lost their glory and died spiritually and politically. Leaving God always brings ruin to those who once walked in His favor.

The people multiplied their sins by crafting idols out of their own silver, following human ideas instead of God's law. They showed affection and honor to lifeless calf statues by kissing them, while turning away from the living God. Human hands can never make something worthy of divine worship.

Because their devotion was so shallow, God announced that Israel would vanish quickly. They would disappear like morning mist, dew burned off by the sun, chaff blown away from a threshing floor, or smoke escaping through a window. Pride built on idols quickly scatters into nothing.

The Lord reminded the people that He had been their God ever since He brought them out of slavery in Egypt. He told them to acknowledge no other deity, because there is no other savior who can truly rescue them. God alone deserves our trust because only He has the power to save.

God cared for Israel when they wandered through the dry, scorched wilderness where nothing could grow. His knowing them meant showing faithful love and providing food and water when they had no way to help themselves. God proves His faithfulness especially when our circumstances seem hopeless.

When Israel arrived in the rich pastures of the promised land, they ate until they were full. Their plenty made them proud and self-reliant, and as a result, they completely forgot the God who had fed them. Prosperity easily leads people to forget their constant need for the Lord.

Because they forgot Him, the Lord warned that He would become like a prowling lion and a leopard hiding beside the road to ambush them. Instead of acting as their protective shepherd, God would execute sudden and irresistible judgment. Forsaking God turns His mighty strength against our stubborn ways.

God compares His coming wrath to an enraged mother bear whose cubs have been stolen, tearing open the chest of its prey. He would allow them to be torn apart and devoured like helpless animals before fierce beasts. God uses these shocking pictures to awaken people to the terror of His righteous anger.

Israel brought destruction upon itself by turning against God, who was its only true helper. Their disaster did not come from a failure on God's part, but entirely from their own stubborn rebellion. Sinners destroy themselves when they push away the only One who can rescue them.

God asks where their kings and princes are now to rescue them when their cities are attacked. Israel had demanded human rulers instead of trusting in the Lord, but those leaders were helpless to save the nation from ruin. Human leaders can never provide the ultimate security that comes only from God.

The Lord gave Israel human kings in His displeasure, beginning with their first king and continuing through the northern rulers, and in His wrath He took them away. God sometimes gives people what they stubbornly demand to show them that self-chosen rulers cannot solve their spiritual problems. Demanding our own desires over God's plan only brings disappointment.

Ephraim's wrongdoing is described as tied up in a bag and kept safely in God's records for judgment. Even though the punishment had not yet arrived, God had not forgotten or overlooked their offenses. Sins that remain unconfessed are carefully stored up until the day of reckoning.

Pangs of trouble would strike the nation suddenly, just like labor pains coming upon an expectant mother. Yet Israel acts like an unwise child who refuses to come out of the womb at the right time, risking death rather than entering new life through repentance. Putting off repentance when God calls brings fatal spiritual danger.

God declares His ultimate power to ransom His people from the grave and liberate them from death itself. He taunts death and Sheol, the place of the dead, as defeated foes, promising that His purpose of deliverance will never be revoked. The apostle Paul quotes these words to celebrate the resurrection of believers through Jesus Christ.

differ.view: Some evangelicals interpret these lines in their original setting as a threat of inescapable doom, where God calls on death to strike Israel without pity, and they view Paul's resurrection quote as an inspired reversal of that original meaning.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars read the questions as a summons for death to release its plagues upon unrepentant Israel, viewing the final line as God refusing to show compassion.

notes.meaning: Even though Ephraim was fruitful and prosperous among its brother tribes, a parching east wind sent by the Lord would sweep in from the desert. This wind refers to the invading Assyrian army, which would dry up their springs of wealth and strip away all their treasures. Earthly riches cannot protect anyone when God's judgment sweeps through.

Samaria, the capital city of northern Israel, must bear the punishment for rebelling against her God. The city would fall in war, suffering the terrible ancient horrors of children dashed against stones and pregnant women ripped open. Turning away from God removes His protection and leaves a people exposed to the cruelty of the world.
